Florence, late August. The workshop has to hire an assistant for September, when Matei and Giulia take over. The third candidate of the day, Chiara Benedetti, comes into Bellini's office.
Good morning, Ms Benedetti. Please have a seat.
Good morning. Thank you for inviting me.
We read your CV with great interest. Tell us a little about your training.
I graduated in Conservation of Cultural Heritage in Bologna. Then I did a six-month internship at the Opificio delle Pietre Dure.
Why would you like to work in our workshop in particular?
Because I followed the Syracuse restoration in the papers. And because, as I wrote in my cover letter, I believe restoration is also a service to the community.
What would you say your strengths are?
I'm precise and patient. My weakness, perhaps, is that I'm sometimes too much of a perfectionist.
(smiles) In a restorer that's not a fault. Do you have any questions for us?
Yes. I'd like to know what my duties would be and whether there's a probationary period.
Three months' probation, then a permanent contract. And on Saturday mornings, the workshop is open to the public. Is that a problem?
On the contrary. I'd like that very much.
Good. We'll let you know by Friday. Thank you for coming.
"Opificio delle Pietre Dure" = Florence's restoration institute
"Le faremo sapere" = we'll let you know

1. The structure of a formal letter
Gentile Dottoressa Marini, / Egregio Signore, / Spettabile Ditta,
Dear Dr Marini, / Dear Sir, / Dear Sirs,
Le scrivo per… / In riferimento al Suo annuncio…
I'm writing to… / With reference to your advertisement…
Mi permetto di… / Le sarei grato se potesse…
May I… / I would be grateful if you could…
In attesa di un Suo cortese riscontro,
Looking forward to hearing from you,
"Gentile" is used for men and women and is the safest choice. "Egregio" is very formal and only for men. "Spettabile" (also written "Spett.le") is for companies and institutions.
In formal letters, polite pronouns and possessives are often written with a capital letter, out of respect:
In speech and in less formal emails, the capital isn't compulsory. But in job applications it makes a good impression.
Nome, cognome, data di nascita, indirizzo, e-mail
Laurea in Conservazione dei Beni Culturali, Università di Bologna
Tirocinio presso l’Opificio delle Pietre Dure (6 mesi)
Watch out for false friends: "la laurea" = university degree (not a "laureate" of a prize); "il tirocinio" = internship; "l’esperienza" is often plural in a CV: "esperienze professionali".
Mi sono laureata in… / Ho svolto un tirocinio presso…
Perché credo che… / Mi interessa molto…
Quali sono i Suoi punti di forza?
Vorrei sapere quali sarebbero le mie mansioni.
La ringrazio per il Suo tempo.
Use the conditional for politeness: "Vorrei sapere…", "Mi piacerebbe…", "Sarebbe possibile…?". It sounds much more elegant than "Voglio sapere".
Don't mix registers: if you begin with "Gentile Dottoressa", don't end with "Un bacio" or "Ciao"!
Looking forward to hearing from you, yours faithfully.

The advertisement had come out in early August, on the Uffizi website and in two specialist magazines: "Restoration workshop in the Oltrarno seeks a restorer with experience of panel paintings. A degree in Conservation of Cultural Heritage is required. Send CV and cover letter." Giulia thought they would get ten replies. Forty-seven arrived.

Matei and Giulia read them all, evening after evening, at the kitchen table, while Viola slept. Some were perfect, written with all the right formulas: "Dear Dr Esposito, I am writing with reference to your advertisement…". Others were less perfect. One candidate had begun with "Dear workshop" and ended with "Big hugs". Another had listed among his skills: "Looking at Caravaggio for hours without getting bored".

"I'd hire this one straight away," Matei had said. "I have that skill too." "Yes, but he can't write a formal letter," Giulia had replied, "and half our work is letters to the Heritage Authority." In the end they chose three for interview: a certain Dr Ferretti from Rome, with a four-page CV; a very experienced restorer from Milan; and Chiara Benedetti, from Bologna, twenty-six, with the simplest and most sincere letter of all.

Graziella wanted her say too. Every evening she came up with the coffee, sat down at the table, put on her glasses and read a few letters aloud, commenting. "This one writes too well: he must be full of himself." "This one has put in a photo with her cat: nice, but the cat doesn't work." "This one's from Prato: never trust anyone from Prato." Matei and Giulia laughed, but in the end they took almost all her opinions into account.

Bellini had asked if he could sit in on the interviews. "I won't ask any questions," he had promised. "I'll just set one test. Just one." He wouldn't say what it was. On the day of the interviews he sat in a corner of the office, his hands in his lap, as silent as an antique piece of furniture. On the wall behind him was Davide's drawing of the trattoria, held up with four drawing pins.

Dr Ferretti arrived punctually, in a jacket and tie, and talked for forty minutes. He talked about his studies, his restorations, his articles, his prizes, his travels. When Giulia asked him why he wanted to work there in particular, he replied that a famous workshop like theirs would be very good for his career. Matei noticed that he had never once said the word "painting".

At the end Bellini stood up and set his test. He took the candidate over to a small fifteenth-century Madonna resting on an easel by the window. "Doctor," he said, "look at it for five minutes. In silence. Then tell me what you saw." Ferretti looked at the painting for thirty seconds, then began talking about the Sienese school, dates, attributions. Bellini thanked him with great courtesy and showed him to the door.

The restorer from Milan was very good and very tired. She had come on the six o'clock train, had three interviews in the same week and kept looking at her phone. In front of the Madonna she stayed silent for the five minutes required, but Giulia saw her check her watch twice. Her answers were correct and precise. But they were the answers of someone already thinking about her next train.

Between one interview and the next Davide had arrived, though he usually came only on Saturdays. He had sat down quietly by the window with his exercise book and started drawing. When Giulia glanced over, she saw he had drawn portraits of the candidates: Ferretti with his mouth open, the lady from Milan with her phone in her hand. Under each one he had written, in small letters, how many seconds they had looked at the Madonna.

Then Chiara Benedetti came in. She was small, with round glasses and a worn leather briefcase. She answered all the questions calmly, using "Lei" with everyone with a naturalness Giulia liked immediately. When Bellini asked her to look at the Madonna, she just said "Gladly", went over to the easel and didn't speak again.

Five minutes went by. Then ten. Bellini said nothing. Chiara didn't move. At last she turned round, almost surprised to see them still there. "I'm sorry," she said. "I lost track of time." "What did you see?" asked Bellini. Chiara hesitated. "I saw that someone has already restored it, a long time ago, with a lot of love and very few means. Here, on the cloak, there's a retouch done with a very small brush. Whoever did it was afraid of making a mistake. You can tell."

A different kind of silence fell over the office. Bellini went over to the painting and looked at the spot Chiara was pointing to. Then he said, in a voice Matei and Giulia had never heard from him: "My grandfather did that retouch, in 1967. With his smallest brush. Nobody, in sixty years, had ever noticed it."

Chiara went red to the tips of her ears. "I didn't know," she stammered. "I'm sorry, I didn't mean to criticise…" "You didn't criticise," Bellini interrupted. "You looked. That's different." Then he asked her where she had learned to look like that. Chiara smiled. "From my grandmother. She was a dressmaker in Bologna. She always used to say: before you touch a fabric, look at it until it speaks to you." Bellini nodded slowly, as if he had heard a password.

Before leaving, Chiara stopped in front of Davide's drawing on the wall. "Who did this?" she asked. "One of our apprentices," Giulia replied. "He's twelve." Chiara looked for a long time at the two transparent men at the top, the one with the brush and the one with the bicycle. "Then you've already found your future," she said. "If you take me on, I'd just like to help you wait for it."

That evening Giulia wrote the letter. She wrote it three times, because she wanted every word to be right. "Dear Dr Benedetti, we are pleased to inform you that your application has been successful. We look forward to seeing you on the first of September at nine o'clock. Yours sincerely." Then, under the signature, in small letters, she added a line no manual of formal letters would have approved: "Bring your glasses. There's a lot of looking here."

Chiara's reply arrived the next day, by email, at seven in the morning. It was a perfect formal letter, with all the right formulas: "Dear Dr Esposito, thank you most sincerely for your letter; I am delighted to accept…". Only the last line wasn't formal at all: "P.S. I always wear my glasses. And from today, a small brush too, just in case." Giulia read it to Bellini, who laughed and said: "Hired."
